questions.question: List five physical properties of metals and give a use that depends on each.
questions.expected_answer: Lustre (shiny): jewellery, mirrors. Good electrical conductor: copper wiring, aluminium power lines. Good heat conductor: pots and pans. Malleable: aluminium foil, roofing sheets, car bodies. Ductile: copper wire, fencing wire. Sonorous: bells. High melting point and strength: steel beams, engine parts.

questions.question: Compare the properties of metals and solid non-metals under the headings appearance, conductivity, effect of hammering and melting point. Name the exceptions mercury and graphite.
questions.expected_answer: Appearance: metals shiny (lustrous); non-metals dull. Conductivity: metals good conductors of heat and electricity; non-metals poor conductors (insulators). Hammering: metals flatten (malleable, ductile); solid non-metals shatter (brittle). Melting point: metals mostly high; non-metals mostly low. Exceptions: mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature; graphite is a non-metal (carbon) that conducts electricity.

questions.question: Explain why silicon is classified as a semi-metal and give two uses. Describe two simple tests to classify an unknown element.
questions.expected_answer: Silicon looks shiny like a metal but is brittle like a non-metal, and it is a semiconductor, conducting electricity better than an insulator but worse than a metal, with conductivity that can be controlled. Uses: computer chips (transistors) in cellphones and computers; solar cells. Tests: place it in a circuit with a cell and bulb; if the bulb lights brightly it is a metal. Tap it gently with a hammer (with eye protection); a metal flattens, a non-metal or semi-metal shatters. Also observe whether it is shiny when scratched.
